chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
title: 101 Ranch and bringing Freddie Keppard's cornet into the district
summary: Dawson recalls O'Neal Lavasheaux's band, then his own five-piece band at Harry Parker's 101 Ranch and how Keppard got a permit to play cornet.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Can you tell us any more about the About the time when the district was running About that time you were talking about Do you remember the different bands that were playing in the district?
Well around about 1904 They had O'Neal Lavish there He had a five piece band He was playing at Few Clothes Right on Franklin Near Iberville
Is that the place that they crossed from the 25? Right across from the 25
They had a fella, a big fella called Few Clothes It was a dance hall
Yeah, I know F.S. He played there

Yeah, yeah, I know Neal Lavish there He played, you know, he was a violin player Oh, he violin That was his band Yeah, it was his band And that fella Few Clothes had his dance hall there And then the next block from there Was Harry Park and Charlie Park Called 101 Ranch And that's where I played there
That must have been around 1907. Harry Parker's dance hall, that's a... Was that the 101 Ranch? 101 Ranch, me and Manetta. Mani Manetta.

Yeah, that was my job. I had Mani Manetta. Who else did you? I had the old man, Umprey. Willie Umprey, the clarinet player, yeah. And I had a Mani Manetta on the piano, and I was playing guitar. That time I was playing guitar. And John Vino on the drum. And... Let's see, we only had five pieces. See, I count five. Mani Manetta, Willie Umprey, John Vino, myself, and the piano.
Did you have a carnet in those days?
No, we didn't have...we didn't have...we didn't have a carnet then.
Didn't use carnet in the district?

No, no, no, no, not around that time. I was the one that...I was the first one that started to bring in the carnet in there. Freddie Kep would come through there with his carnet one night. And Mr. Harry Parker was standing in the door, and Freddie had played a job. It was kind of late. Almost time for us to knock off. And Freddie came in with his trumpet and laid it down, you know. And so Harry Parker would come and ask me what instrument that was. And I told him to do the carnet. They said, well, tell him to go ahead and tune up and play a piece with you. So I told him, I said, well, you know, they don't allow you to blow that instrument around, you know, now around here. He said, oh, he said, tell him to go ahead and...so I asked Fred, I said, you want to play a couple of numbers from the boss wants you to play? He said, well, if he takes care of me, I don't mind. And the police was standing in the door, well, he'd be there every night. So Harry Parker said, oh, go ahead and play. That's all right. They ain't going to do you nothing. They ain't going to put you in jail. I'll be, hold me responsible. Freddie said, all right, boss. And he took his carnet out and tuned up with us and went to play. And it sounds so good, all the women that was beer hustling down at Hunts and Nagels there, they heard about it and they start to leave and the crowd was leaving. They're coming over to Harry Parker's place. Well, after the packed and jam his place, he asked Fred if he wanted to work every night with us. And he said, yes, if you get a permit. So he said, well, I'll go to the mayor, see the mayor tomorrow and I'll get a permit. And you'll be here tomorrow night at the Dawson's Band. And after that, well, he, the next day, Harry Parker went and got a permit for the trumpet. And he worked there with us then from that on. And that's before Joe Oliver then went to Hunts and Nagels. But the next following week, Hunts and Nagels then got Joe Oliver's whole band over there.
Then after I quit, you see, over there went to Joe Oliver. That's all.
